Live showcase

This page is deliberately executable. Each source example is followed directly by the result it produces.

A labelled form 

Form Signup() {
  TextInput Name("Name") {
    placeholder = "Ada";
    required = true;
  }
  Select Interest("Interest") {
    options = ["Tools", "Games", "WebAssembly"];
  }
  Button Join("Join the list");
  Output Confirmation("Ready");
};
Ready

The result above is real generated HTML: labels, inputs, a select, a touch-sized button, and a live output region.

A typed calculator 

Column Calculator() {
  Number Left("Left") { value = 2; }
  Number Right("Right") { value = 3; }
  Button Add("Add") {
    on Click => AddNumbers(Left, Right) -> Answer;
  }
  Output Answer("Waiting...");
};
Waiting...

Press Add above: the generated bridge passes both values to C++ and writes the returned number into Answer.

The calculator and maze use one small executable module. The C++ is ordinary typed behavior: the page declares controls and outputs, while the module owns the calculation and game state.

The same module is shown here as ordinary C++ so it remains readable in the documentation. The executable cpp wasm fence above is what the compiler embeds into this page.

// Calculator behavior.
auto AddNumbers(int32 A, int32 B) -> int32 {
  return A + B;
}

// Maze behavior.
namespace {
int32 MazeX = 1;
int32 MazeY = 1;

auto MazeFrame() -> FString {
  FString Frame =
      "#######\n#.....#\n#.###.#\n#...#.#\n###.#.#\n#...*.#\n#######";
  const auto Index = static_cast<std::size_t>(MazeY * 8 + MazeX);
  Frame[Index] = (MazeX == 4 && MazeY == 5) ? '*' : '@';
  return Frame;
}

auto TryMazeMove(int32 X, int32 Y) -> FString {
  const FString Walls =
      "#######\n#.....#\n#.###.#\n#...#.#\n###.#.#\n#...*.#\n#######";
  if (X >= 0 && X < 7 && Y >= 0 && Y < 7 &&
      Walls[static_cast<std::size_t>(Y * 8 + X)] != '#') {
    MazeX = X;
    MazeY = Y;
  }
  return MazeFrame();
}
} // namespace

auto MoveMazeUp() -> FString { return TryMazeMove(MazeX, MazeY - 1); }
auto MoveMazeLeft() -> FString { return TryMazeMove(MazeX - 1, MazeY); }
auto MoveMazeDown() -> FString { return TryMazeMove(MazeX, MazeY + 1); }
auto MoveMazeRight() -> FString { return TryMazeMove(MazeX + 1, MazeY); }

A tiny playable maze

The same model works for a tiny game loop: state stays in typed C++, while the page owns the controls and the output surface.

Column MazeGame() {
  Output MazeMap("#######\n#@....#\n#.###.#\n#...#.#\n###.#.#\n#...*.#\n#######") {
    class = "maze-board";
  }
  Row MazeControls() {
    class = "maze-controls";
    Button MazeUpButton("↑") {
      class = "maze-up";
      on Click => MoveMazeUp() -> MazeMap;
    }
    Button MazeLeftButton("←") {
      class = "maze-left";
      on Click => MoveMazeLeft() -> MazeMap;
    }
    Button MazeDownButton("↓") {
      class = "maze-down";
      on Click => MoveMazeDown() -> MazeMap;
    }
    Button MazeRightButton("→") {
      class = "maze-right";
      on Click => MoveMazeRight() -> MazeMap;
    }
  }
  Output MazeHint("Reach the star with the touch-sized D-pad.");
};
####### #@....# #.###.# #...#.# ###.#.# #...*.# #######
Reach the star with the touch-sized D-pad.

Result: a real generated output board with touch-sized controls. The maze is intentionally tiny: the point is the shape of the interaction, not a proprietary game engine hidden inside the site generator.

ASCII motion without JavaScript 

Element Orbit() {
  tag = "div";
  class = "ascii-stage";
  Text Frame("S L A M // *");
};
S L A M // *

The result is the animated terminal-style panel below. It is CSS motion over a semantic DOM element, so it works without a runtime and respects reduced-motion preferences.

A responsive canvas declaration 

Canvas Game() {
  width = 1280;
  height = 720;
  responsive = true;
};

The result is a responsive canvas element ready for an application lifecycle. The SDK deliberately leaves drawing to the project or renderer you choose.

What the compiler adds

  • semantic HTML and accessible labels;
  • private component IDs and typed event wiring;
  • responsive base styles and focus states;
  • route, link, asset, and partial validation;
  • optional Emscripten modules and manifests;
  • a complete dist/ directory that can be hosted anywhere.
